title: The Grain Ship and the Seminar Room: Felix Weil, the Argentine Fortune, and the Institute for Social Research
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, born into the grain house
stops.date_confidence: attested; both the English and German encyclopedic entries give this date and this city
stops.campa: Felix José Weil is born in Buenos Aires on the eighth of February, in the same year his father and uncles register the grain house Weil Hermanos y Cia. Hermann Weil, tenth of thirteen children of a Jewish family in the Baden village of Steinsfurt, had apprenticed with the Mannheim grain trader Isidor Weismann, followed two brothers to the United States in 1888, and reached the Rio de la Plata a decade after that. The son is born into a fortune that is still being assembled, denominated in wheat and in freight. Hermann had married Weismann's daughter Rosa in 1896.
suggested_refs: Jeanette Erazo Heufelder, Der argentinische Krösus (biography of Hermann and Felix Weil)

stops.name: Concepción del Uruguay, the birthplace the tradition names
stops.date_confidence: contested: family and regional tradition against the encyclopedic record, which gives Buenos Aires; the conflict is left standing
stops.campa: Upriver from Buenos Aires, on the Uruguay, stands a port town that tradition names as the place of Felix's birth, one of the early nodes of his father's grain buying in Entre Ríos. The English and German reference works give Buenos Aires instead, and no document recovered puts the family in Concepción del Uruguay at all. Two claims sit on the map at once, four hundred kilometres apart, and neither has been made to yield. The town's grain wharves and its river traffic are real enough. Whether a child was carried down from them in February 1898 is not established.
suggested_refs: Parish and civil birth registers of Concepción del Uruguay, Entre Ríos, for February 1898, not consulted

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the house at its height
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the firm's scale; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Within two years the firm has some three thousand employees, subsidiaries in every major European city, and a fleet of sixty ships, making Hermann Weil the largest grain trader in the world. His small son grows up inside this, in a house paid for by a commodity he will never trade. The money that will one day underwrite a Marxist research institute is at this moment being made in the most orthodox manner available on the continent. The wheat of the pampas moves through his father's ledgers to Antwerp, to Rotterdam, to the Balkans.
suggested_refs: Records of Weil Hermanos y Cia., Buenos Aires, not consulted

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Goethe-Gymnasium at nine
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown and defaulted to January
stops.campa: At nine he is put on a ship and sent to Germany for his schooling, entering the Goethe-Gymnasium on the Bahnstrasse, the street later renamed Friedrich-Ebert-Anlage. He arrives with an Argentine childhood and a German surname and is finished in Wilhelmine Frankfurt: Greek, Latin, the whole apparatus for producing a certain kind of man. What he takes out of the Gymnasium is the language, and the city he will hand an institute to sixteen years later. The family business waits for him in Buenos Aires. He will not enter it.
suggested_refs: Goethe-Gymnasium Frankfurt, school records for the years from 1907

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the father comes back from Argentina
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is unknown and the marker sits on the canonical Frankfurt pin rather than on the Zeppelinallee address
stops.campa: The same year, Hermann Weil leaves Argentina for reasons of health. His brother Samuel keeps the Buenos Aires office; the business itself is directed from Rotterdam. He takes a villa at Zeppelinallee 77 in Frankfurt and begins giving grain money away on a scale that requires institutions built to receive it, which is what the son will do sixteen years later in a different key. The sum over the following years is some hundred and twenty million marks, spent on relief foundations, war charities and agricultural research.
suggested_refs: The Hermann Weil villa, Zeppelinallee 77, Frankfurt am Main

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the death of Rosa Weil
stops.date_confidence: date attested exactly; no source names the city of death, and the marker follows the family's Frankfurt residence
stops.campa: Rosa Weil, born Weismann, daughter of the Mannheim trader Hermann had apprenticed under and his wife since 1896, dies of cancer on the sixteenth of April. Felix is fourteen and five years into a German schooling on another continent from where he was born. His father is left a widower with the largest grain business on earth and a growing appetite for philanthropy, and does not remarry. The record gives the date to the day, and no source consulted names the city she died in.
suggested_refs: The Weil family graves, Frankfurt am Main, not located in this pass

stops.name: Tübingen, the promotion forbidden
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, and no source gives the year his Tübingen studies began
stops.campa: He reads political economy at Tübingen through the war and the revolution that ends it, and in 1919 the faculty forbids his promotion to the doctorate on account of his revolutionary politics. The German word the record uses is verboten, which is stronger than refused. He is twenty-one, the son of a man who has been pouring millions into the German war effort's civilian relief, and he has been shut out of a German university for being a red. He packs and goes north to Frankfurt to take the degree there instead.
suggested_refs: Promotion records of the University of Tübingen for 1919, not consulted

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the dissertation on socialization
stops.date_confidence: 1920 given by the English record; the German record dates the Frankfurt doctorate without any year at all
stops.campa: The University of Frankfurt, eight years old and raised on the endowments of the city's merchant houses, gives him the doctorate Tübingen withheld. The dissertation is on socialization: not whether to socialize but the conceptual foundation for doing it, together with a critique of the plans then circulating through the Weimar ministries. It is a rich young man's technical paper on the practical difficulties of abolishing the arrangement that made him rich, and he never writes anything comparable again. The English record dates it 1920. The German record gives the Frankfurt doctorate no year at all.
stops.quote: Socialization: An Attempt at a Conceptual Foundation, with a Critique of the Plans for Socialization
stops.quote_source: Title of Weil's Frankfurt dissertation as rendered in English Wikipedia, 'Felix Weil'; the German original title is unconfirmed
suggested_refs: Felix Weil, doctoral dissertation, University of Frankfurt am Main, 1920

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Karl Korsch and a Marxism outside the parties
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source consulted; placed with the Frankfurt student years by inference only
stops.campa: In the student circles of these years he meets Karl Korsch and studies Marxist economic theory with him. Weil belongs, in Jörg Später's description, to a generation born around the turn of the century into bourgeois and mostly Jewish families and drawn to a philosophical Marxism that stood outside the workers' parties altogether. He has the money to act on that, which almost none of the others do. Korsch will publish Marxismus und Philosophie within three years and be expelled from the German Communist Party for what is in it.
stops.quote: zur Generation der um die Jahrhundertwende geborenen und aus bürgerlichen, meist jüdischen Familien stammenden Intellektuellen, die in den 1920er Jahren von einem philosophischen Marxismus jenseits der Arbeiterparteien angezogen wurden
stops.quote_source: Jörg Später, 'Zuerst kommt die Geldanlage, dann die Theorie', Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, 7 March 2017, p. 10
suggested_refs: Karl Korsch, Marxismus und Philosophie (1923)

stops.name: Argentina, the marriage year
stops.date_confidence: 1921 attested for the marriage and roughly a year for the stay; the sources name only Argentina, no city, and the marker sits on the canonical Buenos Aires pin
stops.campa: He marries Käthe Bachert and takes her to his birth country for about a year, the only extended adult residence he keeps there. The record says Argentinien and stops; it names no city, no house, no business. He is twenty-three, newly doctored, and looking at the pampas his father's ships are emptying into Europe. Käthe will be with him at the Thuringian hotel two years from now, one of the few women in the photographs taken there. The marriage runs to 1929.
suggested_refs: Argentine civil marriage and residence records for Felix and Käthe Weil, 1921-1922, not located

stops.name: Buenos Aires, research on the working class
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish record places these trips in the 1920s without naming years; the date here is a placement, not an attestation
stops.campa: Through the decade he comes back to study the emerging Argentine working class, the first of the two long relationships he keeps with the country of his birth. The second, a decade later, will be fiscal. He is the heir of the largest grain exporter in the republic, doing labour research in the ports and on the estancias that fill its holds. The Spanish-language record is the only one carrying these journeys at all; the German and English accounts of his life pass over them without a word. The ships are his family's; the dockworkers are his subject.
suggested_refs: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Félix Weil', on the Argentine research trips

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the institute founded
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the English record and by the German account of the Arbeitswoche; the German entry on Weil himself dates his co-founder role to 1924 instead, unresolved
stops.campa: On the third of February the Institut für Sozialforschung comes into being at the University of Frankfurt, endowed through a foundation set up by Hermann Weil and his son. Felix has argued for a research institute rather than a party organ, holding that Marxism had to be advanced not only through party politics but scientifically as well. It becomes the only Marxist research institute attached to a German university, and it exists because a grain exporter indulged his son. His father, whose money it is, signs it over.
stops.quote: dass der Marxismus nicht nur parteipolitisch, sondern auch wissenschaftlich vorangebracht werden müsste
stops.quote_source: Süddeutsche Zeitung review notice for Jeanette Erazo Heufelder, Der argentinische Krösus, as digested on Perlentaucher.de
suggested_refs: Foundation deed of the Institut für Sozialforschung, Frankfurt, 1923

stops.name: Geraberg, the First Marxist Work Week
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in the German record, which also fixes the place at Geraberg near Arnstadt; English-language sources put the gathering at Ilmenau instead, and the discrepancy stands
stops.campa: Over Pentecost, for eight days, a couple of dozen Marxists meet at a railway hotel in a Thuringian village, the house belonging to a communist named Friedrich Henne. Karl Korsch has conceived the gathering, Richard Sorge, later the Soviet Union's agent in Tokyo, has handled the invitations, and Weil pays for the whole of it. Georg Lukács is there, and Friedrich Pollock, and Karl August Wittfogel with his wife Rose, and Käthe Weil. The village sits on the north slope of the Thuringian Forest and the nearest thing to a city is Arnstadt.
stops.quote: 1923 finanzierte Weil die von Karl Korsch angeregte Erste Marxistische Arbeitswoche in Geraberg (Thüringen).
suggested_refs: Michael Buckmiller's identification of the Arbeitswoche participants from the surviving photographs
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Felix Weil' (places it at Ilmenau)

stops.name: Geraberg, the photographs and the roster
stops.date_confidence: the eight days run from 20 May; the closing date is calculated, not attested
stops.campa: The Japanese Marxist Fukumoto Kazuo, in Germany to study, photographs the gathering, and his plates become the only reliable roster of who was actually in the room. Michael Buckmiller will later identify nineteen of the roughly twenty-one faces visible in them: Hedda Korsch, Eduard Ludwig Alexander, Konstantin Zetkin, Fritz Sternberg, Heinrich Süßkind among them. The week ends and the participants disperse into the institute founded three months earlier, whose first theory seminar this has been. Weil's own memoirs remember about twenty-five.
suggested_refs: Fukumoto Kazuo's photographs of the Erste Marxistische Arbeitswoche, May 1923

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the institute opens on the Viktoria-Allee
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The building opens on the Viktoria-Allee, the street later renamed Senckenberganlage: library, reading rooms, offices for a staff that will grow to hold most of the names the school is remembered by. Weil, whose money built the rooms, takes no chair and gives no address. Carl Grünberg, brought from Vienna where he had taught Austro-Marxist law for a generation, gives the inaugural address and states plainly that the institute will work by the Marxist research method. He is its first director.
stops.quote: stiftete Weil daher nicht nur im Jahr 1924 großzügig das Institut
stops.quote_source: Süddeutsche Zeitung review notice for Der argentinische Krösus, on Perlentaucher.de; the 1924 in the fragment tracks the opening, the founding decree being dated 3 February 1923
suggested_refs: Carl Grünberg's inaugural address, Frankfurt, 22 June 1924

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the terms of the arrangement
stops.date_confidence: no single date attaches to the arrangement; placed immediately after the opening as a summary of the founding terms
stops.campa: The arrangement settles: the foundation pays, the university houses, the director directs. Weil sits on no faculty and writes nothing the institute issues under its own imprint. Later accounts describe him as an orthodox Marxist who took Marxism for a science and wanted historical and social research on the workers' movement, and he leaves that research to men who will spend the next forty years disagreeing with each other about what it found. His title, on the occasions he needs one, is founder.
stops.quote: Weil himself was an orthodox Marxist, who saw Marxism as scientific; the role of the Institut would be social and historical research mainly on the workers' movement.
suggested_refs: Statutes of the Institut für Sozialforschung and its Stiftung, 1923-1924

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Hermann Weil dies at fifty-nine, thirty-nine years after leaving Baden with two brothers for America and twenty-nine after founding the grain house in Buenos Aires. He has lived to see the institute opened and has never explained publicly why he paid for it. From this point the money keeping the lights on at the Senckenberganlage is the son's rather than the father's, a distinction that matters more to Felix than to anybody drawing a salary out of it. The fortune passes to Felix.
suggested_refs: Hermann Weil's will and the Weil family foundations, Frankfurt am Main

stops.name: Berlin, the money in the Weimar left
stops.date_confidence: the German record dates this only as after 1927; the year here is a placement
stops.campa: Part of the inheritance goes into left-wing cultural work in Berlin during the last Weimar years, in a city where communism is a going concern and money for it is short. Weil funds; he does not direct. A newspaper review notice will one day call him a trusted contact of the Communist International, but that is a reviewer's compression of somebody else's book and nothing consulted corroborates it. What is documented is the pattern rather than the politics: he pays, and other people speak. No recipient of the Berlin money is named anywhere in the record.
suggested_refs: Jeanette Erazo Heufelder, Der argentinische Krösus, on Weil's Berlin funding
sources: Perlentaucher.de review digest for Der argentinische Krösus

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Grünberg's stroke
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Four years into the directorship Carl Grünberg suffers a stroke and cannot go on. He had come from Vienna in his sixties to run a German institute by the Marxist research method, and he leaves it without a valedictory. The Austro-Marxist generation, historians of the labour movement and of its law, is handing over to a younger one that will read psychoanalysis and philosophy as freely as it reads Marx. Friedrich Pollock, Weil's friend since the Thuringian week, takes the place on an interim footing and holds it three years.
suggested_refs: Carl Grünberg's Archiv für die Geschichte des Sozialismus und der Arbeiterbewegung

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the first marriage ends
stops.date_confidence: 1929 attested for the end of the marriage; no source gives a place, and the marker follows the couple's German residence
stops.campa: The marriage to Käthe Bachert ends after eight years. She had gone with him to Argentina in 1921 and sat among the Marxists at the railway hotel in 1923, and after this she leaves the record altogether. Weil will marry five times in the course of his life. Of the four wives who are not Käthe the sources give no names and no dates, in the biography of a man whose finances are documented down to the mark. The place of the divorce is not recorded either.
suggested_refs: German civil marriage registers for Felix Weil after 1929, not located

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Horkheimer takes the chair
stops.date_confidence: 1931 in the German record of the institute, 1930 in the English record of the school; the one-year conflict is unresolved, and no month is given by either
stops.campa: Max Horkheimer becomes director and, in the same act, professor of social philosophy in the university, the two posts fused so that the institute's head sits inside the faculty. He starts bringing in the people the school will be named for: Theodor Adorno, Erich Fromm, Herbert Marcuse. The programme swings away from the archive of the labour movement and toward a critical theory of the whole society. Weil, who paid for an institute of Marxist economics, raises no objection to being handed something else. The German record dates the appointment 1931 and the English record 1930.
suggested_refs: Max Horkheimer's inaugural lecture as professor of social philosophy, Frankfurt, 1931

segments.name: The Money Out Before the People

stops.name: Geneva, the branch at the Labour Office
stops.date_confidence: summer 1932 in the German record of the institute; a parallel account of the same move gives 1933-1934, and the conflict is left standing
stops.campa: The institute opens a branch office at the International Labour Organization in Geneva, in the Centre William Rappard above the lake. Hitler is not yet chancellor. It is a precaution taken by men who can read an election result, and it will turn out to be the measure that saves the endowment, since assets held in Switzerland cannot be seized in Frankfurt. From this summer the institute keeps its money in one country and its library in another. The building above the lake has housed the International Labour Office since 1926.
suggested_refs: Centre William Rappard, Geneva, seat of the International Labour Office from 1926

stops.name: Geneva, the Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested; no day given
stops.campa: In February a new body is constituted in Geneva to hold what the Frankfurt foundation held: the Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales. The Reichstag burns the same month and the arrests begin. The institute's capital leaves Germany before its scholars do. Weil's fortune, made in Argentine grain and settled on a German university nine years earlier, will spend the Nazi period incorporated under Swiss law and paying salaries in New York. The name on the deed is French and the jurisdiction is Swiss. The month and the year are attested and no day is given for it.
suggested_refs: Statutes of the Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales, Geneva, 1933

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the institute closed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of March the building on the Senckenberganlage is closed by the new authorities, six weeks after the seizure of power. A Marxist research institute inside a German university is not a thing the new state intends to leave standing. The endowment is already in Geneva. The staff disperse toward Geneva, toward Paris, and in the end toward New York. Weil is thirty-five and has just watched the one thing he built be shut by police in the city where he went to school.
suggested_refs: Prussian ministry and Frankfurt police files on the closure of the Institut für Sozialforschung, March 1933

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Gestapo takes the building
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In July the Gestapo formally seizes and dissolves the institute's Frankfurt property under the law on the confiscation of communist assets. What is taken is the building, the fittings, the library, the whole German half of the arrangement. What is not taken, because it is no longer in Germany, is the money. The school will go into exile with salaries to pay rather than as a scattering of unemployed lecturers. The law under which the seizure is made is dated the twenty-sixth of May, 1933.
suggested_refs: Gesetz über die Einziehung kommunistischen Vermögens, 26 May 1933

stops.name: Paris, the outpost and the publisher
stops.date_confidence: the German record names the Paris outpost and the Alcan imprint without any year; the date here is a placement in the first exile years
stops.campa: A documentation office is set up at the École normale supérieure under Paul Honigsheim, and the Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung goes on appearing from the house of Félix Alcan, whose Paris imprint is now the journal's publisher. It keeps its German title until 1939, printing Marxist social research in the language of the country that has just outlawed it. The institute has become a German thing published in France on money held in Switzerland by scholars increasingly resident in America. No source consulted gives a year for the Paris office.
suggested_refs: Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung, Paris, Librairie Félix Alcan, 1933-1939

segments.name: Exile, and the Country He Wrote About

stops.name: New York, Columbia takes the institute in
stops.date_confidence: 1934 in the institute's own account, 1935 in the English record of the school; no month in either, and the conflict is unresolved
stops.campa: Columbia University offers the exiled institute a place on Morningside Heights, and most of the staff cross the Atlantic. Horkheimer, Pollock, Adorno, Marcuse, Löwenthal, Fromm: a German research institute reconstituted on an American campus, keeping its name, its director and its Geneva-held endowment. Weil is not among the scholars who move into the offices. He is the reason the offices exist. They arrive into a country still arguing about the Depression in the buildings next door.
suggested_refs: Columbia University records of the Institute of Social Research, Morningside Heights, from 1934
sources: English Wikipedia, 'University of Frankfurt Institute for Social Research'

stops.name: New York, the estate signed over
stops.date_confidence: 1935 attested; the record names only the institute's foundation, which was then Geneva-seated, so this marker's placement in New York is an inference and not an attestation
stops.campa: Weil makes over his personal fortune to the institute's foundation. This is not an endowment being topped up; it is an estate transferred, the whole of what came to him from Hermann in 1927 signed into the body that pays Horkheimer's staff. The record names only the foundation, which by this date is seated in Geneva. The rest of his life will be lived on what stayed outside that transfer, which turns out to be less than a man of his origins would expect, and the last working decade of it on a salary from the United States Air Force. He is thirty-seven.
suggested_refs: Transfer instruments of Felix Weil to the Société Internationale de Recherches Sociales, 1935, not located

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the tax on incomes
stops.date_confidence: the Spanish record places this work in the 1930s without naming years or months; the date is a placement
stops.campa: The institute he founded is by now working out of Morningside Heights, and he spends part of this decade back in Buenos Aires on public finance. The Spanish-language record credits him with a hand in the creation of Argentina's tax on rents and incomes, the fiscal instrument by which the republic began reaching into the earnings of the class his family belonged to. He is the son of the grain house, back in the country of the grain house, helping to write the law that will read its books. Whether anyone in the firm's counting rooms knew whose son was in the ministry is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Félix Weil', on his part in the impuesto a los réditos

stops.name: New York, the journal changes language
stops.date_confidence: the English title ran from 1939 to 1941; a 1935 date for the change circulates and does not survive checking against the run of the journal
stops.campa: The Zeitschrift für Sozialforschung, printed in Paris under its German title through the end of the thirties, becomes Studies in Philosophy and Social Science. The change is not a gesture toward the hosts; France is about to become unavailable as a place to print anything in German. It is the last periodical Weil's fortune carries, and he has never sat on its editorial board. Three volumes appear under the English title before the war and the money together stop it in 1941.
suggested_refs: Studies in Philosophy and Social Science, New York, 1939-1941

stops.name: New York, Argentine Riddle
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; no month given
stops.campa: He publishes Argentine Riddle, issued in Spanish as El enigma argentino, a study of his birth country's political economy written from the United States two years before Perón is elected president. It is the only book he finishes. It is the work of a man who has been reading Argentina from Frankfurt, from Geneva and from New York for twenty years, in the intervals left over from funding other people's reading. Of roughly seventy-seven years of life he will spend some sixteen of them in Argentina, and write more about it than about the Germany that educated him and lost his institute.
suggested_refs: Felix J. Weil, Argentine Riddle (New York, 1944); Spanish edition El enigma argentino

stops.name: California, the last address
stops.date_confidence: 1945 attested for the move; the record gives the state and no city, and the marker sits on Los Angeles for want of anything better
stops.campa: He settles permanently in California and stays. The state is all the record offers: no city, no street, no house. The institute he founded is in New York, the fortune that founded it is inside a Swiss-chartered foundation, and the man himself is on the far coast of a country he reached as a refugee from the country that made him German. From here the biography thins out to dates. He is forty-seven, has been in the United States about a decade, and will spend thirty more years in it.
suggested_refs: California residence and voter records for Felix J. Weil after 1945, not consulted

segments.name: The Relief on the Wall and the Wage

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the institute reopens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The institute is formally reopened on the fourteenth of November in a new building by Hermann Mäckler and Alois Giefer, with Horkheimer at its head again. Adorno and Pollock have come back to West Germany with him; Marcuse, Löwenthal and Kirchheimer have stayed in America. The founder stays in America too. Nobody offers him a post, and nothing in the record suggests he asked for one. The building stands on the Senckenberganlage, where the first one stood.
suggested_refs: The Mäckler and Giefer building of the Institut für Sozialforschung, Senckenberganlage, Frankfurt

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the bronze relief in the entrance hall
stops.date_confidence: the honour is dated to 1963 and tied to his sixty-fifth birthday, which fell on 8 February; the ceremony's own date is not given
stops.campa: On his sixty-fifth birthday the city of Frankfurt awards him its Ehrenplakette, and a bronze relief of his head is fixed in the entrance hall of the institute. Forty years after the endowment the patron is on the wall of the building his father's wheat paid for, facing the people coming in to the seminar rooms. The face is cast in metal in Frankfurt while the man is living in California on what is left of the estate. In Frankfurt he is the financier of the institute, which is how the German record names him whenever it names him at all. The date of the ceremony itself is not recorded.
stops.quote: Bekannt ist er insbesondere als Finanzier des Frankfurter Instituts für Sozialforschung (IfS).
suggested_refs: The bronze portrait relief of Felix Weil, entrance hall of the Institut für Sozialforschung

stops.name: Ramstein Air Base, the major and the tax course
stops.date_confidence: 1969 to 1973 attested for the posting; no months given
stops.campa: At seventy-one, the money gone, Weil takes paid employment: teaching taxation and municipal budget questions to United States Air Force personnel at Ramstein, in the rank of major. He is back in Germany, on a NATO air base in the Palatinate, sixty-two years after the Goethe-Gymnasium and forty-six after the Thuringian hotel where he paid for Lukács and Korsch to argue for eight days. He teaches municipal budgeting to American airmen in the country that confiscated his institute thirty-six years earlier, and draws a wage for it. He holds the post four years.
stops.quote: Der frühere Mäzen Weil war an seinem Lebensabend gezwungen, einer bezahlten Beschäftigung nachzugehen.
suggested_refs: United States Air Force education service records, Ramstein Air Base, 1969-1973

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the lectures of 1970 and 1973
stops.date_confidence: visits attested for 1970 and 1973 with no months; the German phrasing distributes the two invitations between Iring Fetscher and the institute without saying which came first
stops.campa: Twice in these years he comes back to Frankfurt to lecture, once at the invitation of Iring Fetscher and once at the institute's own. He is in his seventies and travelling in from an American air base in the Palatinate to the city where he took the doctorate Tübingen refused him and gave away a fortune. He is a founder returning as a guest, on a lecture invitation like anybody else. The visits survive as two lines in a German encyclopedia entry. What he said on either occasion is preserved in no source consulted.
suggested_refs: Iring Fetscher's Frankfurt seminars and the Institut für Sozialforschung lecture programme, 1970 and 1973

stops.name: Dover Air Force Base, the history of flight
stops.date_confidence: the Ramstein posting ends in 1973 and the Dover teaching follows it; no start date is given anywhere
stops.campa: The last post is at Dover in Delaware, teaching the history of aviation to cadets of the Civil Air Patrol. He is seventy-five, a lifelong Marxist in the costume of an American officer, explaining to teenagers how two world wars and a cold one moved the world about, with aeroplanes for the example. His biographer calls the image the fitting closing picture at the end of a contradictory life. The passage that describes him doing it names the cadets and not the base.
stops.quote: Die Vorstellung, dass 1975 ein Marxist in der Verkleidung eines US-Offiziers den jungen Kadetten der Civil Air Patrol die durch Weltkriege und Kalten Krieg ausgelösten globalen politischen Verschiebungen am Beispiel der Luftfahrtgeschichte erklärte, gehört zu den Eigentümlichkeiten dieser ideologiegetränkten Zeit und ist das passende Schlussbild am Ende eines widersprüchlichen Lebens.

stops.name: Dover, the heart attack
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by both the English and German records; the Spanish record's birth year of 1895 makes him eighty here and is not consistent with the 1898 given elsewhere
stops.campa: He dies of a heart attack on the eighteenth of September, seventy-seven years old, in a small state capital on the American east coast, four years into a memoir begun in 1971 and never finished. Fischer Verlag will decline to publish it. No source consulted records where he is buried, not a cemetery and not a plot. The man who paid for the building the Frankfurt School worked in has no known grave. The Spanish encyclopedia entry, working from a birth year of 1895, calls him eighty at his death.

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the memoirs in the Karmeliterkloster
stops.date_confidence: the deposit is undated in the record; placed after his death by inference
stops.campa: Parts of the unfinished memoirs come to rest in the Institut für Stadtgeschichte in the Karmeliterkloster on the Karmelitergasse, a few streets from where the old Judengasse ran and a mile from the institute. A publisher having refused them, the city archive takes them in. The archive holding them belongs to the city that gave him its plaque in 1963. They are the only account in his own voice of a life spent paying for other people's voices, and they stop before they reach the end.
